title: 1 Couette flow

1 Couette flow
Consider Couette flow, that is, the flow between two parallel plates with the upper plate moving at a velocity \(V_{\max}\). The temperature field measured in this flow is
\[
t\ag{x_i}\ = T_0 + \Delta T\, x_1.
\tag{1}\]
What is the rate of change of temperature experienced by the material particle that is located at \(\bsf{x} = (0, 0)\) at time \(\bs{\tau} = 1\,\rm{s}\)? The deformation mapping corresponding to this flow is
\(\bsf{x}\ag{\cdot}\ag{\cdot}: \mathbb{R}\times B\to B\), \(B=\left\{ (X_1,X_2)\in \mathbb{R}^2~|~0<X_{2}<h\right\}\), \[
\begin{aligned}
x_{1}[\tau]\ag{X_i}&=X_1+V_{\rm max}\left(1-\left(\frac{X_2}{h}\right)^2\right)\tau,\\
x_{2}\ag{\tau}\ag{X_i}&=X_2,
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}\]

1.0.0.1 Solution 1
Let us refer to an equation Eq. 2. Let \(^P\bsf{X}\) be the material particle that is located \(\bsf{x} = (0, 0)\) at time \(\bs{\tau} = 1\,\rm{s}\). Let the material temperrature field be \(T\ag{\tau}\ag{X_i}\). One way to get the rate change of temperature experienced by the material particle \(^P\bsf{X}\) is to get the material time derivative of the temperrature field. \[
\frac{\partial}{\partial \tau}T\ag{\tau,X_i}=T'[\tau]\ag{X_i}
\tag{3}\] and then compute \(T'[1]\ag{^P X_i}\).
We need two things the material temperature field and the \(^P\bsf{X}\). The materials temperature field is easy to get, \[
T[\tau]\ag{X_i}=T_0+\Delta T \left(X_1+V_{\rm max}\left(1-\left(\frac{X_2}{h}\right)^2\right)\tau\right)
\tag{4}\] The material field corresponding to the material time derivative of the temperature field is \[
T'[\tau]\ag{X_i}=\Delta T V_{\rm max}\left(1-\left(\frac{X_2}{h}\right)^2\right)
\tag{5}\]
To get \(^{P}\bsf{X}\) we need the inverse deformation map. The inverse deformation map is \(\bsf{X}\ag{\cdot}\ag{\cdot}: \mathbb{R}\times B\to B\), \(B=\left\{ (X_1,X_2)\in \mathbb{R}^2~|~0<X_{2}<h\right\}\), \[
\begin{aligned}
X_{1}[\tau]\ag{X_i}&=x_1-V_{\rm max}\left(1-\left(\frac{x_2}{h}\right)^2\right)\tau,\\
X_{2}\ag{\tau}\ag{X_i}&=x_2,
\end{aligned}
\tag{6}\]
From the inverse deformation map we get the \(^P \bsf{X}=(-V_{\rm max},0)\).Substituting this result in Eq. 5 we get the rate of temperature change experienced by the material particle to be \[
\Delta T V_{\rm max}
\]
Also using the inverse deformation map we get the material temperature field to be \[\begin{equation}
\end{equation}\]


1.0.0.2 Solution 2
There is an alternate way to do this. This by using the spacial velocity field. The material velocity field is \[
\begin{align}
V_1\ag{\tau}\ag{X_i}&=V_{\rm max}\left(1-\left(\frac{X_2}{h}\right)^2\right),\\
V_2\ag{\tau}\ag{X_i}&=0.
\end{align}
\]
The spatial velocity field is \[
\begin{align}
v_1\ag{\tau}\ag{x_i}&=V_{\rm max}\left(1-\left(\frac{x_2}{h}\right)^2\right),\\
v_2\ag{\tau}\ag{x_i}&=0.
\end{align}
\]
Now we apply the formular for the material time derivative to the spatial temperature field, \[\begin{align}
\frac{Dt}{D\tau}&=t_{,\tau}+v_{i}t_{,i}.
\end{align}\] We know that the first term is zero. The second terms \[
{\text{grad}}\, t=\Delta T \,\bsf{E}_1.
\] Thus we have that
\[
v_i t_{,i}=V_{\rm max} \Delta T\left(1-\left(\frac{x_2}{h}\right)^2\right),
\] which at the spatial point \(\bsf{x}=(0,0)\) at \(\tau=1\) computes to be \[
v_i t_{,i}=V_{\rm max} \Delta T,
\]
Thus the material time derivative of the temperature field at the time instance \(\tau\) and \(\bsf{x}=(0,0)\) is \[V_{\rm max} \Delta T\].

title: 1 Deformation and Motion
text:
The previous section described reference and current bodies as well as Lagrangian and Eulerian coordinates of a material particle. However, we still need to describe the motion of the material body, that is the map between the reference and deformed bodies. The reference configuration maps the material body to the reference body, and the current configuration maps the material body to the current body. We would also like to have a map between the reference body and deformed bodie(s).

Definition 1 
The motion is a map \(\bs{\varphi} : \bs{\mathcal{B}}_{\rm{R}} \times \b{T} \to \mathbb{E}\) that takes in a material particle \(\bs{X}\in \bs{\mathcal{B}}_{\rm R}\) and a time \(\tau \in \b{T}\), and returns the spatial position \(\bs{\varphi}\sqpr{\bs{X}, \bs{\tau}} = \bs{x}\) occupied in \(\mathbb{E}\) at the time instance \(\bs{\tau}\).

Note: We model time as a one dimensional vector space and denote it with \(\b{T}\).

Definition 2 
The deformation map \(\bs{\varphi}_{\tau} : \bs{\mathcal{B}}_{\rm{R}} \to \mathbb{E}\) takes in a material particle \(\bs{X}\in \bs{\mathcal{B}}_{\rm R}\) and return the spatial position \(\bs{\varphi}_{\tau}\sqpr{\bs{X}}\) occupied in \(\mathbb{E}\) at the time instance \(\bs{\tau}\). We often use \(\bs{x}_{\tau}\) as an abbreviation for \(\bs{\varphi}_{\tau}\sqpr{\bs{X}}\).

The motion can be thought of as the collection of all deformation maps at all time instances. When we consider a single time instance, that is \(\bs{\varphi}\sqpr{\cdot, \bs{\tau}}\), we obtain the deformation map \(\bs{\varphi}_{\tau}\).


In continuum mechanics we will be interested in a wide class of possible deformation maps, but we will place some conditions on \(\bs{\varphi}_{\tau}\). We will say that \(\bs{\varphi}\) is an admissible deformation map if and only if

\(\bs{\varphi}_{\tau}\) is defined for all \(\bs{X}\in \bs{\mathcal{B}}_{\rm R}\)
\(\bs{\varphi}_{\tau}\) is injective, except perhaps at the boundary of \(\bs{\mathcal{B}}_{\rm R}\) (such as to avoid interpenetration)
\(\bs{\varphi}_{\tau}\) is continuously differentiable, expect perhaps at the boundary of \(\bs{\mathcal{B}}_{\rm R}\) (such as to avoid cracks, dislocations)

If the deformation map is well defined for the entire domain and injective, then it is possible to be more specific about the codomain. Particularly, the codomain is the set \(\bs{\mathcal{B}}_{\tau} \subset \b{R}\), which is the current body in the physical Euclidean space. Then the deformation map \(\bs{\varphi}_{\tau} : \bs{\mathcal{B}}_{\rm{R}} \to \bs{\mathcal{B}}_{\tau}\) is also surjective and therefore bijective.
Since it is bijective, there exists a well defined inverse map. This is true for finite dimensional maps between vector spaces of the same dimension. Therefore, it is possible to define the inverse map \(\bs{\varphi}^{-1} : \bs{\mathcal{B}}_{\tau} \to \bs{\mathcal{B}}_{\rm R}\) such that \(\bs{\varphi}^{-1}_{\tau}\sqpr{\bs{x}}:=\) gives the material particle \(\bs{X}\) that is located at \(\bs{x}\) at time instance \(\bs{\tau}\). Clearly \(\bs{\varphi}_{\tau}\sqpr{\bs{\varphi}_{\tau}^{-1}\sqpr{\bs{x}}}=\bs{x}\).




Recall the nondimensionalization map \(\msf{U} : \bs{\mc{B}}_{\rm{R}} \to \b{R}^{3}\). We define the components of the deformation map as follows \[
\begin{align}
\bs{\varphi}_{\tau}\sqpr{\bs{X}} &= \varphi_{i\tau}\sqpr{\msf{U}\sqpr{\bs{X}}}\bs{e}_i,
\end{align}
\]
where \[
\varphi_{i\tau}:\mathbb{R}^3\to \mathbb{R}
\]
and \(\pr{\msf{U}\sqpr{\bs{X}}}_{j} = X_j\). Specifically, \(X_{j}=\bs{X}\cdot \bs{E}_j\). The functions \(\varphi_{i\tau}\) are called the components of the deformation map. We can also define the deformation map by defining the map, \[
\begin{align}
\bs{\varphi}_{\tau}: B_{\rm R} \to \mathbb{E},
\end{align}
\]
where \[
\bs{\varphi}_{\tau}\sqpr{X_1,X_2,X_3}=\varphi_{i\tau}\sqpr{X_{1},X_{2},X_{3}}\bs{e}_i
\]
This map is different from the map \(\bs{\varphi}_{\tau} :\bs{\mathcal{B}}_{\rm R}\to \mathbb{E}\).
Clearly, when \(X_i\) are the components/co-ordinates of \(\bs{X}\) w.r.t \(\bs{E}_i\), \(\bs{\varphi}_{\tau}\sqpr{X_1,X_2,X_3}=\bs{\varphi}_{\tau}\sqpr{\bs{X}}\). Despite using the same symbols, it will be clear from context as to which map we are talking about. In many books you will see \(x_i\) being used as an alias for \(\varphi_{i}\sqpr{X_1,X_2,X_3}\).
When we are considering a specific deformation map at a time instance \(\bs{\tau}\), we will omit writing the \(\tau\) as a subscript. In such a case the above paragraph can be written as, \[
\begin{align}
\bs{\varphi}\sqpr{\bs{X}}=\varphi_{i}\sqpr{X_{1}, X_{2}, X_{3}}\bs{e}_i,
\end{align}
\]
where \(\varphi_{i} : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}\) and \(\msf{U}\sqpr{\bs{X}} = \pr{\bs{X}\cdot\bs{e}_{1}, \bs{X}\cdot\bs{e}_{2}, \bs{X}\cdot\bs{e}_{3}} = \pr{X_1, X_2, X_3}\). The functions \(\varphi_{i}\) are called the components of the deformation map.
It follows from the above introduced notation that the spatial location occupied by the material particle \(\bs{X}\) is \(x_i \bs{e}_i\). Thus, \(\bs{x}=x_i\bs{e}_i\).





Let \(B_{\rm R}= \set{(X_{1}, X_{2}, X_{3})}{0 \leq X_{i} \leq L, ~i=1,2,3}\), where \(L \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\). Consider a deformation map \(\bs{\varphi}:B_{\rm R}\to \mathbb{E}\). The deformation consists in strectching each edge of the cube in the \(a^\text{th}\) direction by a factor of \(\lambda_a\). \(\lambda_a\in (0, \infty)\), which is expressed as \[
\begin{align}
x_1&=\lambda_1X_1,
\\
x_2&=\lambda_2X_2,
\\
x_3&=\lambda_3 X_3.
\end{align}
\]
The values \(\lambda_1\),\(\lambda_2\), and \(\lambda_3\) are called the stretch rations.



For \(\gamma\in \mathbb{R}\), the deformation map \[
\begin{align}
x_1&=X_1+\gamma X_2\\
x_2&=X_2\\
x_3&=X_3
\end{align}
\]
is called pure shear in the \(\bs{X}_1-\bs{X}_2\) plane, and \(\gamma\) is the shear deformation.



Another type of two dimensional deformation has the following form, \[
\begin{align}
x_1&=X_1\\
x_2&=X_2\\
x_3&=\varphi_3(X_1,X_2)
\end{align}
\] In this case the deformation is only in the \(\bs{E}_3\) direction.



We often describe deformations of bodies in two-dimensions. One possible type of essentially two-dimensional deformation is, \[
\begin{align}
x_1&=\varphi_1(X_1,X_2)\\
x_2&=\varphi_2(X_1,X_2)\\
x_3&=X_3
\end{align}
\]
Because there is no deformation along the \(\bs{E}_3\) direction, these types of deformations are called “plane strain”.

1 Vector Spaces
text:
Definition 1 Real vector space
A real vector space is a set \(\mc{V}\) over the real numbers \(\b{R}\) on which the two operations of \(\cdot + \cdot : \mc{V}\times \mc{V} \to \mc{V}\) (addition) and \(\cdot * \cdot: \mc{V}\times \b{R}\to \mc{V}\) (scalar multiplication) are defined and satisfies the following properties:


Additive commutativity
\(\bs{u}+\bs{v}=\bs{v}+\bs{u}\) for all \(\bs{u},\bs{v} \in \mc{V}\)
Additive associativity
\(\bs{u}+(\bs{v}+\bs{z})= (\bs{u}+\bs{v})+\bs{z}\) for all \(\bs{u}, \bs{v}, \bs{z} \in \mc{V}\)
Scalar multiplicative associativity
\((ab)\bs{v} = a(b\bs{v})\) for all \(v \in \mc{V}\) and all \(a,b \in \b{R}\)
Zero (null) element
There exists a zero element \(\bs{0}_{\mc{V}}\) or simply \(\bs{0}\) when there is no risk of confusion, such that \(\bs{0} + \bs{v} = \bs{v}\) for all \(\bs{v} \in \mc{V}\)
Additive inverse
For every \(\bs{v} \in \mc{V}\), there exists \(\bs{v}' \in \mc{V}\) such that \(\bs{v} + \bs{v}' = \bs{0}\)
Scalar multiplicative identity
\(1\bs{v} = \bs{v}\) for all \(\bs{v} \in \mc{V}\)
Distributivity of scalar over vector addition
\(a(\bs{u}+\bs{v}) = a\bs{u} + a\bs{v}\) for all \(a \in \b{R}\) and all \(\bs{u},\bs{v} \in \mc{V}\)
Distributivity of scalar addition over vector
\((a+b)\bs{v} = a\bs{v} + b\bs{v}\) for all \(a,b \in \b{R}\) and all \(\bs{v} \in \mc{V}\)

We can show identities such as \(-1 * \bs{v}=\bs{v}'\) and \(0 * \bs{v}=\bs{0}\) from the above axioms.
\[
\begin{align}
\pr{1+(-1)}\bs{v}&=1*\bs{v}+(-1)*\bs{v}\\
\pr{0}\bs{v}&=1*\bs{v}+(-1)*\bs{v}\\
\bs{0}&=1*\bs{v}+(-1)*\bs{v}\\
\bs{0}&=\bs{v}+(-1)*\bs{v}\\
(-1) * \bs{v}&=\bs{v}'
\end{align}
\]
\[
\begin{align}
\pr{1+0} * \bs{v}&=1 * \bs{v}+(0) * \bs{v}\\
\pr{1} * \bs{v}&=1 * \bs{v}+(0) * \bs{v}\\
\bs{v}&=\bs{v}+(0) * \bs{v}\\
\bs{0}&=(0)*\bs{v}\\
\end{align}
\]
When there is no confusion we will skip explicitly writing \(*\), so expressions such as \(a * \pr{b \bs{v}}=\pr{ab}  *  \bs{v}\) will appear as \(a\pr{b \bs{v}}=\pr{ab}  \bs{v}\)

Examples:

\(\b{R}^{1} = \b{R}\)
\(\b{R}^{2} = \cpr{\pr{a, b} : a, b \in \b{R}}\)
\(\b{P}^{k}= \cpr{p : \b{R} \ra \b{R} ~\vert~ p(x) = a_{0}+a_{1}x+\dots+a_{k}x^{k}}\)


Definition 2 Subspace
A subset \(\mc{U}\) of \(\mc{V}\) is a subspace of \(\mc{V}\) if it is also a vector space using the same addition and scalar operation as on \(\mc{V}\). Namely, \(\mc{U}\) is a subspace only if it satisfies, \(\bs{0} \in \mc{U}\), \(\bs{u} + \bs{v} \in \mc{U}\) for all \(\bs{u} \in \mc{U}\) and \(a \bs{u} \in \mc{U}\) for all \(a \in \b{R}\) and \(\bs{u} \in \mc{U}\).




A list of length \(n\) is an ordered collection of \(n\) elements. We denote lists without parenthesis as \(\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n}\). By definition, a list has finite length.
A linear combination of a list of vectors \(\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n} \in \mc{V}\) is a vector of the form \(a_{1} \bs{v}_{1} + ... + a_{n} \bs{v}_{n}\) where \(a_{1},...,a_{n} \in \b{R}\).
The span of a list of vectors \(\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n} \in \mc{V}\) is the set of all linear combinations of the form \(a_{1} \bs{v}_{1} + ... + a_{n} \bs{v}_{n}\) where \(a_{1},...,a_{n} \in \b{R}\) and is denoted by \(\text{span}\pr{\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n}}\). If \(\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n}\) spans \(\mc{V}\), then \(\text{span}\pr{\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n}} = \mc{V}\)

Definition 3 Finite dimensional vector space
A vector space \(\mc{V}\) is finite dimensional if some list of vectors \(\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n} \in \mc{V}\) spans the space.

A list of vectors \(\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n} \in \mc{V}\) is said to be linearly independent if its linear combination is \(\bs{0}\) iff the scalars \(a_{1},...,a_{n}\) are all \(0\). On the contrary, a list is linearly dependent if a linear combination is \(\bs{0}\) for some list of scalars \(a_{1},...,a_{n}\) where not all are \(0\). In a finite-dimensional vector space, the length of each linearly independent list of vectors is less than or equal to the length of every spanning list of vectors.

Definition 4 Basis
A basis of \(\mc{V}\) is a linearly independent list of vectors \(\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n} \in \mc{V}\) that spans \(\mc{V}\). An equivalent definition is that the list \(\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n} \in \mc{V}\) is basis of \(\mc{V}\) iff every \(\bs{v} \in \mc{V}\) can be written as a unique linear combination of the list.

Every finite dimensional vector space \(\mc{V}\) has a basis. The dimension of \(\mc{V}\) is given by the length of any of its basis. All bases of a finite dimensional vector space have the same length. A proper subspace always has a smaller dimension than the larger space. We will denote finite dimensional vector spaces with a superscript to indicate the dimension, for example, \(\mc{V}^{n}\) or \(P^{k}\).




Definition 5 Inner product
An inner product on \(\mc{V}\) is an operation \(\apr{\cdot, \cdot} : \mc{V} \times \mc{V} \rightarrow \b{R}\) such that for all \(\bs{u}, \bs{v}, \bs{z} \in \mc{V}\) and for \(a \in \b{R}\), we have

\(\apr{\bs{u}, \bs v} = \apr{\bs v, \bs u}\)
\(\apr{\bs u, \bs v + a \bs z} = \apr{\bs u, \bs v} + a \apr{\bs u, \bs z}\)
\(\inpd{\bs u}{\bs u} \geq 0\)
\(\inpd{\bs u}{\bs u} = 0\) iff \(\bs{u} = \bs{0}\)


An real inner product space is a real vector space on which an inner product is defined. An inner product is not a requirement of a vector space.

Definition 6 Norm
A norm on \(\mc{V}\) is an operation \(\norm{\cdot} : \mc{V} \rightarrow \b{R}_{\geq 0}\) such that such that for all \(\bs{u}, \bs{v} \in \mc{V}\) and for \(a \in \b{R}\), we have

\(\norm{a \bs u} = \abs{a} \norm{\bs u}\)
\(\norm{\bs u + \bs v} \leq \norm{\bs u} + \norm{\bs v}\)
\(\norm{\bs u} = 0\) iff \(\bs u = \bs 0\)


A vector space equipped with a norm is called a normed vector space. To be more precise, we denote a norm of vector space \(\mc{V}\) as \(\norm{\cdot}_{\mc{V}}\) and similarly for norms of other vector spaces. Every inner product induces a norm. The induced norm is given by \(\norm{\bs u} = \sqrt{\inpd{\bs u}{\bs u}}\).




Definition 7 An Euclidean vector space \(\b{E}\) is a finite dimensional real inner product space.

We denote an \(n\) dimensional Euclidean space by \(\b{E}^{n}\). We denote the Euclidean inner product between two vectors \(\bs{a}, \bs{b}\) by \(\bs{a} \cdot \bs{b}\).

Definition 8 An affine point space \(\mc{E}\) is a set of points on which the addition of two points is not defined, there is no unique zero element, and the difference between two points belongs to the associated Euclidean vector space.

We denote an \(n\) dimensional affine point space by \(\mc{E}^{n}\). The term point is reserved for elements of \(\mc{E}\) and the term vector for elements of \(\b{E}\).

Definition 9 Euclidean space
We denote the pair \(\pr{\mc{E}^{n}, \b{E}^{n}}\) as an Euclidean space, to mean an affine point space such that the associated vector space is an Euclidean vector space. Choosing a point \(o \in \mc{E}^{n}\) which we call the origin in \(\mc{E}^{n}\), a point \(x \in \mc{E}^{n}\) corresponds to a vector \(\bs{x} \in \b{E}^{n}\) iff \(o + \bs{x} = x\).




To manipulate and work with vectors, we would like to assign them components. Let \(\mc{F}= (1,\dots,n)\). Let a list of vectors \(\bs{e}_{i}, \dots, \bs{e}_{n} \in \b{E}^{n}\) form a basis for \(\b{E}^{n}\). Then for a vector \(\bs{x} \in \b{E}^{n}\), we can write \(\bs{x} = \sum_{i \in \mc{F}} x_{i} \bs{e}_{i}\). The components of \(\bs{x}\) w.r.t. to the basis \(\bs{e}_{i}, \dots, \bs{e}_{n}\) are the real numbers \(x_{i},\dots,x_{n}\). We give the components a column matrix representation. For example, the components of a vector \(\bs{x} \in \b{E}^{3}\) w.r.t a basis \(\bs{e}_{1},\bs{e}_{2},\bs{e}_{3}\) may be written as \[
    \begin{bmatrix}
    a \\ b \\ c
    \end{bmatrix}
\]
where \(a, b, c \in \b{R}\). The following is not a meaningful statement: \[
\bs{x} =
    \begin{bmatrix}
    a \\ b \\ c
    \end{bmatrix}
\]
Instead, we write
\[
    \bs{x} = \sum_{i=1}^{3} x_{i} \bs{e}_{i}
\]
The column matrix representation of the components is only meaningful after an appropriate basis has been chosen, not otherwise.

title: 1 Vector Spaces
text:
Definition 1 Real vector space
A real vector space is a set \(\mc{V}\) over the real numbers \(\b{R}\) on which the two operations of \(\cdot + \cdot : \mc{V}\times \mc{V} \to \mc{V}\) (addition) and \(\cdot * \cdot: \mc{V}\times \b{R}\to \mc{V}\) (scalar multiplication) are defined and satisfies the following properties:


Additive commutativity
\(\bs{u}+\bs{v}=\bs{v}+\bs{u}\) for all \(\bs{u},\bs{v} \in \mc{V}\)
Additive associativity
\(\bs{u}+(\bs{v}+\bs{z})= (\bs{u}+\bs{v})+\bs{z}\) for all \(\bs{u}, \bs{v}, \bs{z} \in \mc{V}\)
Scalar multiplicative associativity
\((ab)\bs{v} = a(b\bs{v})\) for all \(v \in \mc{V}\) and all \(a,b \in \b{R}\)
Zero (null) element
There exists a zero element \(\bs{0}_{\mc{V}}\) or simply \(\bs{0}\) when there is no risk of confusion, such that \(\bs{0} + \bs{v} = \bs{v}\) for all \(\bs{v} \in \mc{V}\)
Additive inverse
For every \(\bs{v} \in \mc{V}\), there exists \(\bs{v}' \in \mc{V}\) such that \(\bs{v} + \bs{v}' = \bs{0}\)
Scalar multiplicative identity
\(1\bs{v} = \bs{v}\) for all \(\bs{v} \in \mc{V}\)
Distributivity of scalar over vector addition
\(a(\bs{u}+\bs{v}) = a\bs{u} + a\bs{v}\) for all \(a \in \b{R}\) and all \(\bs{u},\bs{v} \in \mc{V}\)
Distributivity of scalar addition over vector
\((a+b)\bs{v} = a\bs{v} + b\bs{v}\) for all \(a,b \in \b{R}\) and all \(\bs{v} \in \mc{V}\)

We can show identities such as \(-1 * \bs{v}=\bs{v}'\) and \(0 * \bs{v}=\bs{0}\) from the above axioms.
\[
\begin{align}
\pr{1+(-1)}\bs{v}&=1*\bs{v}+(-1)*\bs{v}\\
\pr{0}\bs{v}&=1*\bs{v}+(-1)*\bs{v}\\
\bs{0}&=1*\bs{v}+(-1)*\bs{v}\\
\bs{0}&=\bs{v}+(-1)*\bs{v}\\
(-1) * \bs{v}&=\bs{v}'
\end{align}
\]
\[
\begin{align}
\pr{1+0} * \bs{v}&=1 * \bs{v}+(0) * \bs{v}\\
\pr{1} * \bs{v}&=1 * \bs{v}+(0) * \bs{v}\\
\bs{v}&=\bs{v}+(0) * \bs{v}\\
\bs{0}&=(0)*\bs{v}\\
\end{align}
\]
When there is no confusion we will skip explicitly writing \(*\), so expressions such as \(a * \pr{b \bs{v}}=\pr{ab}  *  \bs{v}\) will appear as \(a\pr{b \bs{v}}=\pr{ab}  \bs{v}\)

Examples:

\(\b{R}^{1} = \b{R}\)
\(\b{R}^{2} = \cpr{\pr{a, b} : a, b \in \b{R}}\)
\(\b{P}^{k}= \cpr{p : \b{R} \ra \b{R} ~\vert~ p(x) = a_{0}+a_{1}x+\dots+a_{k}x^{k}}\)


Definition 2 Subspace
A subset \(\mc{U}\) of \(\mc{V}\) is a subspace of \(\mc{V}\) if it is also a vector space using the same addition and scalar operation as on \(\mc{V}\). Namely, \(\mc{U}\) is a subspace only if it satisfies, \(\bs{0} \in \mc{U}\), \(\bs{u} + \bs{v} \in \mc{U}\) for all \(\bs{u} \in \mc{U}\) and \(a \bs{u} \in \mc{U}\) for all \(a \in \b{R}\) and \(\bs{u} \in \mc{U}\).

title: 1 Vector Spaces
text:
A list of length \(n\) is an ordered collection of \(n\) elements. We denote lists without parenthesis as \(\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n}\). By definition, a list has finite length.
A linear combination of a list of vectors \(\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n} \in \mc{V}\) is a vector of the form \(a_{1} \bs{v}_{1} + ... + a_{n} \bs{v}_{n}\) where \(a_{1},...,a_{n} \in \b{R}\).
The span of a list of vectors \(\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n} \in \mc{V}\) is the set of all linear combinations of the form \(a_{1} \bs{v}_{1} + ... + a_{n} \bs{v}_{n}\) where \(a_{1},...,a_{n} \in \b{R}\) and is denoted by \(\text{span}\pr{\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n}}\). If \(\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n}\) spans \(\mc{V}\), then \(\text{span}\pr{\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n}} = \mc{V}\)

Definition 3 Finite dimensional vector space
A vector space \(\mc{V}\) is finite dimensional if some list of vectors \(\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n} \in \mc{V}\) spans the space.

A list of vectors \(\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n} \in \mc{V}\) is said to be linearly independent if its linear combination is \(\bs{0}\) iff the scalars \(a_{1},...,a_{n}\) are all \(0\). On the contrary, a list is linearly dependent if a linear combination is \(\bs{0}\) for some list of scalars \(a_{1},...,a_{n}\) where not all are \(0\). In a finite-dimensional vector space, the length of each linearly independent list of vectors is less than or equal to the length of every spanning list of vectors.

Definition 4 Basis
A basis of \(\mc{V}\) is a linearly independent list of vectors \(\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n} \in \mc{V}\) that spans \(\mc{V}\). An equivalent definition is that the list \(\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n} \in \mc{V}\) is basis of \(\mc{V}\) iff every \(\bs{v} \in \mc{V}\) can be written as a unique linear combination of the list.

Every finite dimensional vector space \(\mc{V}\) has a basis. The dimension of \(\mc{V}\) is given by the length of any of its basis. All bases of a finite dimensional vector space have the same length. A proper subspace always has a smaller dimension than the larger space. We will denote finite dimensional vector spaces with a superscript to indicate the dimension, for example, \(\mc{V}^{n}\) or \(P^{k}\).

title: 1 Vector Spaces
text:
Definition 5 Inner product
An inner product on \(\mc{V}\) is an operation \(\apr{\cdot, \cdot} : \mc{V} \times \mc{V} \rightarrow \b{R}\) such that for all \(\bs{u}, \bs{v}, \bs{z} \in \mc{V}\) and for \(a \in \b{R}\), we have

\(\apr{\bs{u}, \bs v} = \apr{\bs v, \bs u}\)
\(\apr{\bs u, \bs v + a \bs z} = \apr{\bs u, \bs v} + a \apr{\bs u, \bs z}\)
\(\inpd{\bs u}{\bs u} \geq 0\)
\(\inpd{\bs u}{\bs u} = 0\) iff \(\bs{u} = \bs{0}\)


An real inner product space is a real vector space on which an inner product is defined. An inner product is not a requirement of a vector space.

Definition 6 Norm
A norm on \(\mc{V}\) is an operation \(\norm{\cdot} : \mc{V} \rightarrow \b{R}_{\geq 0}\) such that such that for all \(\bs{u}, \bs{v} \in \mc{V}\) and for \(a \in \b{R}\), we have

\(\norm{a \bs u} = \abs{a} \norm{\bs u}\)
\(\norm{\bs u + \bs v} \leq \norm{\bs u} + \norm{\bs v}\)
\(\norm{\bs u} = 0\) iff \(\bs u = \bs 0\)


A vector space equipped with a norm is called a normed vector space. To be more precise, we denote a norm of vector space \(\mc{V}\) as \(\norm{\cdot}_{\mc{V}}\) and similarly for norms of other vector spaces. Every inner product induces a norm. The induced norm is given by \(\norm{\bs u} = \sqrt{\inpd{\bs u}{\bs u}}\).

title: 1 Vector Spaces
text:
Definition 7 An Euclidean vector space \(\b{E}\) is a finite dimensional real inner product space.

We denote an \(n\) dimensional Euclidean space by \(\b{E}^{n}\). We denote the Euclidean inner product between two vectors \(\bs{a}, \bs{b}\) by \(\bs{a} \cdot \bs{b}\).

Definition 8 An affine point space \(\mc{E}\) is a set of points on which the addition of two points is not defined, there is no unique zero element, and the difference between two points belongs to the associated Euclidean vector space.

We denote an \(n\) dimensional affine point space by \(\mc{E}^{n}\). The term point is reserved for elements of \(\mc{E}\) and the term vector for elements of \(\b{E}\).

Definition 9 Euclidean space
We denote the pair \(\pr{\mc{E}^{n}, \b{E}^{n}}\) as an Euclidean space, to mean an affine point space such that the associated vector space is an Euclidean vector space. Choosing a point \(o \in \mc{E}^{n}\) which we call the origin in \(\mc{E}^{n}\), a point \(x \in \mc{E}^{n}\) corresponds to a vector \(\bs{x} \in \b{E}^{n}\) iff \(o + \bs{x} = x\).

title: 1 Vector Spaces
1 Change of basis
text:
Let \(\bs{x} \in \b{E}^{3}\) and let \(\{\hat{\bs{E}}_{i}\}_{i=1,2,3}\) and \(\{\hat{\bs{F}}_{i}\}_{i=1,2,3}\) be two orthornal bases for \(\b{E}^{3}\). The question is, would the components of \(\bs{x}\) w.r.t the bases be the same? That is, would
\[
\begin{align}
\bs{x} &= x_i \hat{\bs{E}}_i = \tilde{x}_i \hat{\bs{F}}_i \\
x_{i}&\stackrel{?}{=}\tilde{x}_{i}
\end{align}
\]
In general, the answer is no. Typically, in a different basis the components of \(\bs{x}\) will be different. This is same as measuring the size of an object using a scale that in centimeter unit and another scale which is units of inches. Thus, we will have
\[
\begin{align}
\bs{x}&=y_1 \hat{\bs{F}}_1+y_2 \hat{\bs{F}}_2+y_3 \hat{\bs{F}}_3\\
\bs{x}&=y_i \hat{\bs{F}}_i,
\end{align}
\] i.e.,
\[
\begin{align}
[\bs{x}]_{\{\hat{\bs{F}}\}_{i=1,2,3}}&=
\left[
\begin{array}{c}
y_1\\
y_2\\
y_3
\end{array}
\right]
\end{align}
\]
and typically \(x_i \not= y_i\).
The question now arrises, if we know \(x_i\) how do we find \(y_i\)? The answer to this question involves the change of basis matrix \([Q]\), such that,
Since \(\{\hat{\bs{E}}\}_{i=1,2,3}\) is a basis, and hence each of \(\hat{\bs{F}}_j\) can be written as a linear combination of \(\{\hat{\bs{E}}\}_{i=1,2,3}\).
\[
\begin{align}
\hat{\bs{F}}_1
&=
Q_{11}\hat{\bs{E}}_1+
Q_{21}\hat{\bs{E}}_2+
Q_{31}\hat{\bs{E}}_3
\\
\hat{\bs{F}}_2
&=
Q_{12}\hat{\bs{E}}_1+
Q_{22}\hat{\bs{E}}_2+
Q_{32}\hat{\bs{E}}_3
\\
\hat{\bs{F}}_3
&=
Q_{13}\hat{\bs{E}}_1+
Q_{23}\hat{\bs{E}}_2+
Q_{33}\hat{\bs{E}}_3
\end{align}
\]
The above set of equations can be compactly be written as:
\[
\begin{align}
\hat{\bs{F}}_j&=Q_{ij}\hat{\bs{E}}_i
\end{align}
\]
\[
\begin{align}
\left[\hat{\bs{F}}_1\right]_{\{\hat{\bs{E}}\}_{i=1,2,3}}&
&=
\left[
\begin{array}{c}
Q_{11}\\
Q_{21}\\
Q_{31}
\end{array}
\right]
\end{align}
\]
\[
\begin{align}
\left[\hat{\bs{F}}_2\right]_{\{\hat{\bs{E}}\}_{i=1,2,3}}&
&=
\left[
\begin{array}{c}
Q_{12}\\
Q_{22}\\
Q_{32}
\end{array}
\right]
\end{align}
\]
\[
\begin{align}
\left[\hat{\bs{F}}_3\right]_{\{\hat{\bs{E}}\}_{i=1,2,3}}&
&=
\left[
\begin{array}{c}
Q_{13}\\
Q_{23}\\
Q_{33}
\end{array}
\right]
\end{align}
\]
In summary we can write, \[
\begin{align}
Q=
\left[
\begin{array}{lcr}
\left[\hat{\bs{F}}_1\right]_{\{\hat{\bs{E}}\}_{i=1,2,3}} &
\left[\hat{\bs{F}}_2\right]_{\{\hat{\bs{E}}\}_{i=1,2,3}}
&
\left[\hat{\bs{F}}_3\right]_{\{\hat{\bs{E}}\}_{i=1,2,3}}
\end{array}
\right]
\end{align}
\]
Now let’s try to find the components \(x_i\) from \(y_i\) of a general vector \(\bs{x}\).
Derivation 1
\[ \begin{align}
\bs{x}&=x_i \hat{\bs{E}}_i\\
\bs{x}&=y_i \hat{\bs{F}}_i\\
\hat{\bs{F}}_i&=
Q_{ji}\hat{\bs{E}}_j\\
\bs{x}&=y_i Q_{ji}\hat{\bs{E}}_j\\
x_j&=y_iQ_{ji}\\
x_j&=Q_{ji}y_i\\
x_i&=Q_{ij}y_j\\
\end{align}
\]
\[ \begin{align}
\left[
\begin{array}{c}
x_1\\
x_2\\
x_3
\end{array}
\right]
=
\left[
\begin{array}{lcr}
Q_{11} & Q_{12} & Q_{13} \\
Q_{21} & Q_{22} & Q_{23} \\
Q_{31} & Q_{32} & Q_{33} \\
\end{array}
\right]
\left[
\begin{array}{c}
y_1\\
y_2\\
y_3
\end{array}
\right]
\end{align}
\]
Derivation 2
\[ \begin{align}
\bs{x}&=x_i \hat{\bs{E}}_i\\
\bs{x}&=y_i \hat{\bs{F}}_i\\
\hat{\bs{F}}_i&=
Q_{ji}\hat{\bs{E}}_j\\
\bs{x}&=y_i Q_{ji}\hat{\bs{E}}_j\\
\end{align}
\]
Recall that \(\bs{x}=x_1 \hat{\bs{E}}_1+x_2 \hat{\bs{E}}_2+x_3 \hat{\bs{E}}_3\), which can be compactly be written as \(\bs{x}=x_p \hat{\bs{E}}_p\). Thus, we have
\[
\begin{align}
x_p \hat{\bs{E}}_p&= Q_{ji} y_i\hat{\bs{E}}_j\\
x_p \hat{\bs{E}}_p&= Q_{ij} y_j\hat{\bs{E}}_i\\
(x_p \hat{\bs{E}}_p)\cdot \hat{\bs{E}}_q&= (Q_{ij} y_j\hat{\bs{E}}_i)\cdot \hat{\bs{E}}_q\\
(x_p \hat{\bs{E}}_p\cdot  \hat{\bs{E}}_q)&= (Q_{ij} y_j)\hat{\bs{E}}_i\cdot \hat{\bs{E}}_q\\
(x_p \delta_{pq})&= (Q_{ij} y_j)\delta_{iq}\\
x_q &= Q_{qj} y_j\\
x_i &= Q_{ij} y_j\\
\end{align}
\]
Examples from AL notes. Now let’s assume that
\[
\begin{align}
\hat{\bs{E}}_i=P_{ji}\hat{\bs{F}}_j
\end{align}
\]
Following the same steps as before we arrive at the equation, \[
\begin{align}
y_i &= P_{ij} x_j\\
\end{align}
\]
Combining the results, \(y_i = P_{ij} x_j\) and \(x_i = Q_{ij} x_j\) we have that,
\[
\begin{align}
y_i &= P_{ij} Q_{jk}y_k\\
\delta_{im}y_m &= P_{ij} Q_{jk}y_k\\
\delta_{im}y_m -P_{ij} Q_{jk}y_k&=0\\
(\delta_{ik} -P_{ij} Q_{jk})y_{k}&=0\\
\delta_{ik} -P_{ij} Q_{jk}&=0\\
\end{align}
\]
The last equation can be written as \[
\begin{align}
[P][Q]&=[I],
\end{align}
\]
which implies that \([P]\) is the left inverse of \([Q]\).
\[
\begin{align}
x_i &= Q_{ij} P_{jk}x_k\\
\delta_{ik}x_k &= Q_{ij} P_{jk}x_k\\
\delta_{ik}x_k -P_{ij} Q_{jk}x_k&=0\\
(\delta_{ik} -Q_{ij} P_{jk})x_{k}&=0\\
\delta_{ik} -Q_{ij} P_{jk}&=0\\
\end{align}
\]
The last equation can be written as \[
\begin{align}
[Q][P]&=[I],
\end{align}
\]
which implies that \([P]\) is also the right inverse of \([Q]\).

Combining the results, \(y_i = P_{ij} x_j\) and \(x_i = Q_{ij} x_j\) we have that,
\[
\begin{align}
y_i &= P_{ij} Q_{jk}y_k\\
\delta_{im}y_m &= P_{ij} Q_{jk}y_k\\
\delta_{im}y_m -P_{ij} Q_{jk}y_k&=0\\
(\delta_{ik} -P_{ij} Q_{jk})y_{k}&=0\\
\delta_{ik} -P_{ij} Q_{jk}&=0\\
\end{align}
\]
The last equation can be written as \[
\begin{align}
[P][Q]&=[I],
\end{align}
\]
which implies that \([P]\) is the left inverse of \([Q]\).
\[
\begin{align}
x_i &= Q_{ij} P_{jk}x_k\\
\delta_{ik}x_k &= Q_{ij} P_{jk}x_k\\
\delta_{ik}x_k -P_{ij} Q_{jk}x_k&=0\\
(\delta_{ik} -Q_{ij} P_{jk})x_{k}&=0\\
\delta_{ik} -Q_{ij} P_{jk}&=0\\
\end{align}
\]
The last equation can be written as \[
\begin{align}
[Q][P]&=[I],
\end{align}
\]
which implies that \([P]\) is also the right inverse of \([Q]\).

title: 1 Vector and Tensor Components
text:
Henceforth, the Einstein summation convention will be employed.


A vector can be written as a linear combination of a basis, that is a list of linearly independent vectors the span the space. We are typically interested in vectors that belong to \(\b{E}^{n}\).

Definition 1 Orthogonal vectors
Two vectors \(\bs{u}, \bs{v} \in \b{E}^n\) are orthogonal if \(\bs{u} \cdot \bs{v} = 0\).


Definition 2 Orthonormal basis
An orthonormal basis is a basis whose elements are mutually orthogonal and have a unit norm.

We typically denote orthonormal basis vectors with a tophat, for example \(\{\hat{\bs{E}}_{i}\}_{i=1,2,3}\). Further, we will typically make use of orthonormal basis vectors unless specified otherwise.
Let \(\{\hat{\bs{E}}_{i}\}_{i=1,2,3}\) form an orthonormal basis for \(\b{E}^{3}\). That is any vector \(\bs{u} \in \b{E}^{3}\) can be written as a linear combination of these basis vectors.
\[
\begin{align}
\bs{x}&=x_1 \hat{\bs{E}}_1+ x_2 \hat{\bs{E}}_2+ x_3 \hat{\bs{E}}_3\\
\bs{x}&=x_i \hat{\bs{E}}_i
\end{align}
\]
\[
\begin{align}
[\bs{x}]_{\{\hat{\bs{E}}_{i}\}_{i=1,2,3}}&=
\left[
\begin{array}{c}
x_1\\
x_2\\
x_3
\end{array}
\right]
\end{align}
\]
Let \(\{\hat{\bs{F}}_{i}\}_{i=1,2,3}\) form another orthonormal basis for \(\b{E}^{3}\). Then,
\[
\begin{align}
\bs{x}&=\tilde{x}_1 \hat{\bs{F}}_1+ \tilde{x}_2 \hat{\bs{F}}_2+ \tilde{x}_3 \hat{\bs{F}}_3\\
\bs{x}&=\tilde{x}_i \hat{\bs{F}}_i
\end{align}
\]
\[
\begin{align}
[\bs{x}]_{\{\hat{\bs{F}}_{i}\}_{i=1,2,3}}&=
\left[
\begin{array}{c}
\tilde{x}_1\\
\tilde{x}_2\\
\tilde{x}_3
\end{array}
\right]
\end{align}
\]
Notice that the components differ when the chosen basis differs. Additionally, for clarity, the matrix representation of the components may include a subscript denoting the basis. The following are equivalent representations of the vector:
\[
\begin{align}
\bs{x} = x_{i} \hat{\bs{E}}_{i} = \tilde{x}_{i} \hat{\bs{F}}_{i}
\end{align}
\]
The question is, are the components \(x_{i}\) and \(\tilde{x}_i\) the same? In general no. However, a relation between the two represenation can be determined using a change of basis, which will be discussed in a later section.



Say \(\bs{T} : \b{E}^{n} \ra \b{E}^n\) is a tensor. Then we define its components \(T_{ij}\) w.r.t. to the two bases \(\hat{\bs{E}}_i\) and \(\hat{\bs{F}}_i\) as
\[
\begin{align}
T_{ij}=\hat{\bs{F}}_i\cdot(\bs{T} \hat{\bs{E}}_j)
\end{align}
\]
Typically, we chose both bases to be the same to simplify our study. That is, the components of \(\bs{T}\) w.r.t the basis \(\hat{\bs{E}}_i\) is given by \[
\begin{align}
T_{ij}=\hat{\bs{E}}_i\cdot(\bs{T} \hat{\bs{E}}_j)
\end{align}
\]
Let \(\bs{T} : \b{E}^{3} \ra \b{E}^3\) be a tensor. We define the matrix representation of \(\bs{T}\) as the \(3\times 3\) matrix that we denote as \(\left[\bs{T}\right]\) that satisfies the following equation \[\begin{align}
\left[ \bs{T}\right]
\left[ \bs{a}\right]&=\left[ \bs{T}\bs{a}\right]
\end{align}
\]
for all \(\bs{a}\in \mathbb{E}^3\). Let \(\bs{T}\bs{a}=\bs{b}\), where \(\bs b = b_i \hat{\bs{E}}_i\). The matrix representation of \(\bs{b}\) is,
\[
\begin{equation}
\left[\bs{b}\right]=
\left[
\begin{array}{c}
b_1\\
b_2\\
b_3\\
\end{array}
\right]
\end{equation}
\]
Then we have that, \[
\begin{align}
\left[ \bs{T}\right]
\left[ \bs{a}\right]&=\left[ \bs{b}\right]\\
\end{align}
\]
Let \(T_{ij}\) be the \(i-j^{\text{th}}\) component of the matrix \(\left[\bs{T}\right]\), i.e., \(T_{ij}=\left[\bs{T}\right]_{ij}\). More explicitly, \[
\begin{align}
\left[\bs{T}\right]&=
\left[
\begin{array}{ccc}
T_{11} && T_{12} && T_{13} \\
T_{21} && T_{22} && T_{23} \\
T_{31} && T_{32} && T_{33} \\
\end{array}
\right]
\end{align}
\]
\[
\begin{align}
\left[
\begin{array}{ccc}
T_{11} && T_{12} && T_{13} \\
T_{21} && T_{22} && T_{23} \\
T_{31} && T_{32} && T_{33} \\
\end{array}
\right]
\left[
\begin{array}{c}
a_1\\
a_2\\
a_3\\
\end{array}
\right]
&=
\left[
\begin{array}{c}
b_1\\
b_2\\
b_3\\
\end{array}
\right]
\end{align}
\]
or equivalently, \[
\begin{align}
T_{11}a_1 + T_{12}a_2 + T_{13}a_3 = b_1\\
T_{21}a_1 + T_{22}a_2 + T_{23}a_3 = b_2\\
T_{31}a_1 + T_{32}a_2 + T_{33}a_3 = b_3\\
\end{align}
\]


Motivating example
Let \(\bs{T}\) be a tensor that transforms the specific vectors \(\bs{a}\) and \(\bs{b}\) as follows:
\[
\begin{align}
\bs{T}\bs{a} = \bs{a} + 2\bs{b}, \\
\bs{T}\bs{b} = \bs{a} - \bs{b}.
\end{align}
\]
Given a vector \(\bs{c} = 2\bs{a} + \bs{b}\), find \(\bs{T}\bs{c}\).
Solution
Using the linearity property of tensors, we have \[
\begin{align}
\bs{T}\bs{c} = \bs{T}(2\bs{a} + \bs{b})=2\bs{T}\bs{a} + \bs{T}\bs{b} = 2(\bs{a} + 2\bs{b}) + (\bs{a} - \bs{b}) = 3\bs{a} + 3\bs{b}.
\end{align}
\]
So let us start by defining the Matrix \[
\begin{align}
\left[Q\right]
&=
\left[
\begin{array}{ccc}
Q_{11} && Q_{12} && Q_{13}  \\
Q_{21} && Q_{22} && Q_{23}  \\
Q_{31} && Q_{32} && Q_{33}
\end{array}
\right]
\end{align}
\]
\[
\begin{align}
\bs{T}\hat{\bs{E}}_1&=Q_{11}\hat{\bs{E}}_1+Q_{21}\hat{\bs{E}}_2+Q_{31}\hat{\bs{E}}_3\\
\bs{T}\hat{\bs{E}}_2&=Q_{12}\hat{\bs{E}}_1+Q_{22}\hat{\bs{E}}_2+Q_{32}\hat{\bs{E}}_3\\
\bs{T}\hat{\bs{E}}_3&=Q_{13}\hat{\bs{E}}_1+Q_{23}\hat{\bs{E}}_2+Q_{33}\hat{\bs{E}}_3\\
\end{align}
\]
\[
\begin{align}
\bs{T}\bs{a}&=\bs{T}\left(a_1\hat{\bs{E}}_1+a_2\hat{\bs{E}}_2+a_3\hat{\bs{E}}_3\right)\\
&=\bs{T}\left(a_1\hat{\bs{E}}_1\right)+\bs{T}\left(a_2\hat{\bs{E}}_2\right)+\bs{T}\left(a_3\hat{\bs{E}}_3\right)\\
&=a_1\left(\bs{T}\hat{\bs{E}}_1\right)+a_2 \left(\bs{T}\hat{\bs{E}}_2\right)+a_3\left(\bs{T}\hat{\bs{E}}_3\right)\\
\end{align}
\]
\[
\begin{align}
\bs{T}\bs{a}
&=a_1\left(\bs{T}\hat{\bs{E}}_1\right)+a_2 \left(\bs{T}\hat{\bs{E}}_2\right)+a_3\left(\bs{T}\hat{\bs{E}}_3\right)\\
&=a_1\left(Q_{11}\hat{\bs{E}}_1+Q_{21}\hat{\bs{E}}_2+Q_{31}\hat{\bs{E}}_3\right)+a_2 \left(Q_{12}\hat{\bs{E}}_1+Q_{22}\hat{\bs{E}}_2+Q_{32}\hat{\bs{E}}_3\right)+a_3\left(Q_{13}\hat{\bs{E}}_1+Q_{23}\hat{\bs{E}}_2+Q_{33}\hat{\bs{E}}_3\right)
\end{align}
\]
\[
\begin{align}
\bs{T}\bs{a}
&=\left(Q_{11}a_1\hat{\bs{E}}_1+Q_{21}a_1\hat{\bs{E}}_2+Q_{31}a_1\hat{\bs{E}}_3\right)+ \left(Q_{12}a_2\hat{\bs{E}}_1+Q_{22}a_2\hat{\bs{E}}_2+Q_{32}a_2\hat{\bs{E}}_3\right)+\left(Q_{13}a_3\hat{\bs{E}}_1+Q_{23}a_3\hat{\bs{E}}_2+Q_{33}a_3\hat{\bs{E}}_3\right)
\\
&=
\left(
Q_{11}a_1+
Q_{12}a_2+
Q_{13}a_3\right)\hat{\bs{E}}_1
+
\left(
Q_{21}a_1+
Q_{22}a_2+
Q_{23}a_3\right)\hat{\bs{E}}_2
+
\left(
Q_{31}a_1+
Q_{32}a_2+
Q_{33}a_3
\right)\hat{\bs{E}}_3
\end{align}
\]
\[\begin{align}
\left[\bs{T}\bs{a}\right]
&=
\left[
  \begin{array}{c}
  Q_{11}a_1+Q_{12}a_2+Q_{13}a_3\\
  Q_{21}a_1+Q_{22}a_2+Q_{23}a_3\\
  Q_{31}a_1+Q_{32}a_2+Q_{33}a_3
  \end{array}
\right]
\\
\left[\bs{b}\right]&=
\left[
  \begin{array}{ccc}
    Q_{11} && Q_{12} && Q_{13} \\
    Q_{21} && Q_{22} && Q_{23} \\
    Q_{31} && Q_{32} && Q_{33}
  \end{array}
\right]
\left[
  \begin{array}{c}
    a_1\\
    a_2\\
    a_3
  \end{array}
\right]
\\
\left[
\begin{array}{c}
b_1\\
b_2\\
b_3\\
\end{array}
\right]&=
\left[
  \begin{array}{ccc}
    Q_{11} && Q_{12} && Q_{13} \\
    Q_{21} && Q_{22} && Q_{23} \\
    Q_{31} && Q_{32} && Q_{33}
  \end{array}
\right]
\left[
  \begin{array}{c}
    a_1\\
    a_2\\
    a_3
  \end{array}
\right]
\end{align}
\]
which proves That \[
\begin{equation}
\left[
\bs{T}
\right]=
\left[Q\right]
\end{equation}
\]
Example
Obtain the matrix for the tensor \(\bs{T}\) that transforms the base vectors as follows
\[
\begin{align}
\bs{T}\bs{e}_1 &= 4\bs{e}_1 + \bs{e}_2, \\
\bs{T}\bs{e}_2 &= 2\bs{e}_1 + 3\bs{e}_3,  \\
\bs{T}\bs{e}_3 &= -\bs{e}_1 + 3\bs{e}_2 + \bs{e}_3,
\end{align}
\]
Solution
By the definition above,
\[
\begin{align}
\left[\bs{T}\right]
&=
\left[
\begin{array}{ccc}
4 && 2 && -1  \\
1 && 0 && 3  \\
0 && 3 && 1
\end{array}
\right]
\end{align}
\]

Example
Obtain the matrix for the tensor that transforms the base vectors as follows:
\[
\begin{align}
\bs{T}\bs{e}_1 &= \bs{e}_1 + 2\bs{e}_2 + 3\bs{e}_3,  \\
\bs{T}\bs{e}_2 &= 4\bs{e}_1 + 5\bs{e}_2 + 6\bs{e}_3,  \\
\bs{T}\bs{e}_3 &= 7\bs{e}_1 + 8\bs{e}_2 + 9\bs{e}_3.   
\end{align}
\]
Solution
By inspection,
\[
\begin{align}
\left[\bs{T}\right]
&=
\left[
\begin{array}{ccc}
1 && 2 && 3  \\
4 && 5 && 6  \\
7 && 8 && 9
\end{array}
\right]
\end{align}
\]
This example emphasizes again the convention we use to write the matrix of a tensor: The component of \(\bs{T}\bs{e}_{1}\) fills the first column, the component of \(\bs{T}\bs{e}_{2}\) fills the second column, and so on. The reason for this choice of convention will become obvious in the next section.

Example: Reflection across a plane
Let \(\bs{T}\) transform every vector into its mirror image with respect to a fixed plane; if \(\bs{e}_1\) is normal to the reflection plane (\(\bs{e}_{2}\) and \(\bs{e}_{3}\) are parallel to this plane), find a matrix of \(\bs{T}\).
Solution
Because the normal to the reflection plane is transformed into its negative, and vectors parallel to the place are not altered, we have
\[
\begin{align}
\bs{T}\bs{e}_1 = -\bs{e}_1, \bs{T}\bs{e}_2 = \bs{e}_2, \bs{T}\bs{e}_3 = \bs{e}_3
\end{align}
\]
which corresponds to
\[
\begin{align}
\left[\bs{T}\right]
&=
\left[
\begin{array}{ccc}
-1 && 0 && 0  \\
0 && 1 && 0  \\
0 && 0 && 1
\end{array}
\right]_{\bs{e}_i}.
\end{align}
\]

Example: 2D Rotation
Let \(\bs{R}\) correspond to a right-hand rotation of a rigid body about the \(x_3\)-axis by an angle \(\theta\). Find a matrix of \(\bs{R}\).
Solution
From the figure, it is clear that
\[
\begin{align}
\bs{R}\bs{e}_1 &= \cos\theta\bs{e}_1 + \sin\theta\bs{e}_2, \\
\bs{R}\bs{e}_2 &= -\sin\theta\bs{e}_1 + \cos\theta\bs{e}_2, \\
\bs{R}\bs{e}_3 &= \bs{e}_3.
\end{align}
\]
which corresponds to
\[
\begin{align}
\left[\bs{R}\right]
&=
\left[
\begin{array}{ccc}
\cos\theta && \sin\theta && 0  \\
\sin\theta && \cos\theta && 0  \\
0 && 0 && 1
\end{array}
\right]_{\bs{e}_i}.
\end{align}
\]

Example: Stretching
Write the tensor \(\bs{T}\), defined by the equation \(\bs{T}\bs{a} = \alpha\bs{a}\), where \(\alpha\) is a constant and \(\bs{a}\) is arbitrary, in terms of the identity tensor, and find its components.
Solution
Using the identity tensor, we can write \(\alpha\bs{a}\) as \(\alpha\bs{I}\bs{a}\), so that
\[
\begin{align}
\bs{T}\bs{a} = \alpha\bs{a} = \alpha\bs{I}\bs{a}.
\end{align}
\]
Since \(\bs{a}\) is arbitrary, therefore,
\[
\begin{align}
\bs{T} = \alpha\bs{I}
\end{align}
\]
The components of this tensor are clearly \(T_{ij} = \alpha\delta_{ij}\).



If \(\hat{\bs{E}}_i\) is an orthonormal basis, it can be shown that
\[
\begin{align}
\bs{T}&=T_{ij} \, \hat{\bs{E}}_{i}\otimes \hat{\bs{E}}_{j}
\tag{Dyadic basis}
\end{align}
\]
Let \[
\begin{align}
\bs{T}\bs{c}&=\bs{d}\\
(T_{ij} \, \hat{\bs{E}}_{i}\otimes \hat{\bs{E}}_{j})\bs{c}&=\bs{e}
\end{align}
\]
We are going to find the components of \(\bs{e}\) and \(\bs{d}\) and show that they are one and the same. Since \(\bs{c}\) is arbitrary this goes to prove that \(\bs{T}\) and \(T_{ij}\hat{\bs{E}}_{i}\otimes \hat{\bs{E}}_{j}\) are one and the same.
Components of \(\bs{e}\) \[
\begin{align}
\bs{e}&=(T_{ij}\hat{\bs{E}}_{i}\otimes \hat{\bs{E}}_{j})\bs{c}\\
&=
(T_{ij}\hat{\bs{E}}_{i}\otimes \hat{\bs{E}}_{j})(c_k\hat{\bs{E}}_k)\\
&=
T_{ij} c_k(\hat{\bs{E}}_{i}\otimes \hat{\bs{E}}_{j})\hat{\bs{E}}_k\\
&=
T_{ij} c_k(\hat{\bs{E}}_{i}( \hat{\bs{E}}_{j}\cdot\hat{\bs{E}}_k))\\
&=
T_{ij} c_k(\hat{\bs{E}}_{i}\delta_{jk})\\
&=
T_{ij} c_j\hat{\bs{E}}_{i}
\end{align}
\]
From the last equation it follows that
\[
\begin{align}
\bs{e}\cdot\hat{\bs{E}}_j&=T_{ik}c_k\hat{\bs{E}}_i\cdot\hat{\bs{E}}_j\\
e_j&=T_{ik}c_k\delta_{ij}\\
e_j&=T_{jk}c_k\label{eq:eComponents}\\
\end{align}
\]
Components of \(\bs{d}\)
From the definition of the matrix definition of \(\bs{T}\), which is \([\bs{T}]\) it follows that
\[
\begin{align}
\left[\bs{T}\right]\left[\bs{c}\right]&=\left[\bs{d}\right] \label{eq:MatrixFrom}
\end{align}
\]
where \[
\begin{align}
\left[\bs{c}\right]_{i}&=c_{i}=\bs{c}\cdot \hat{\bs{E}}_i\\
\left[\bs{d}\right]_{j}&=d_{j}=\bs{d}\cdot \hat{\bs{E}}_j
\end{align}
\]
In Einstein notation \(\eqref{eq:MatrixFrom}\) reads,
\[
\begin{align}
d_i&=T_{ij}c_j\label{eq:dComponents}
\end{align}
\]
If follows from \(\eqref{eq:eComponents}\) and \(\eqref{eq:dComponents}\) that \(\bs{e}\) and \(\bs{d}\) are the same, from which it follows that \(\bs{T}\) and \(T_{ij}\hat{\bs{E}}_{i}\otimes \hat{\bs{E}}_{j}\) are one and the same.

text:
For the time being, we forgo a more precise and thorough discussion of tensors and identify them as linear maps between Euclidean vector spaces for our purposes.

Definition 1 Tensors
We refer to linear maps \(\brm{T} \in \mc{L}\pr{\b{E}^{n}, \b{F}^n}\) as tensors, where \(\b{E}^{n}\) and \(\b{F}^{n}\) are Euclidean vector spaces.

Consequentially, the previous discussion on linear maps is applicable to tensors. Important tensors that we will study in continuum mechanics include the deformation gradient tensor, velocity gradient tensor, strain tensors, stress tensors, stiffness tensors, and many more. Since tensors are linear maps, the set of all tensors between two vector spaces is also a vector space.
Some Important Tensors

Definition 2 Identity tensor
Let \(\brm{I} : \b{E}^n \ra \b{E}^n\) be such that \[
    \brm{I} \bs{v} = \bs{v}
\] for all \(\bs v \in \b{E}^n\). Then \(\brm{I}\) is called the identity tensor.

The identity tensor (previously defined as the identity map) maps every vector to itself.

Definition 3 Null tensor
Let \(\bs 0 : \b{E}^n \ra \b{F}^n\) be such that \[
    \bs{0} \bs{v} = \bs{0}_{\b F}
\] for all \(\bs v \in \b{E}^n\). Then \(\bs 0\) is called the null tensor.


Definition 4 Transpose of a tensor
The transpose of a tensor \(\brm{T}\) is the tensor \(\brm{T}^{\msf{T}}\) that obeys the following rule \[
\bs{u}\cdot\pr{\brm{T} \bs{v}} = \pr{\brm{T}^{\msf T} \bs{u}} \cdot \bs{v}
\] for all \(\bs u, \bs v \in \b E^{n}\)

Properties of Transposes
\[  
\begin{array}{ll}
\pr{i} & \tp{\pr{\tp{\brm{A}}}} = \brm{A} \\
\pr{ii} & \tp{\pr{\brm{A} \brm{B}}} = \tp{\brm{B}} \tp{\brm{A}} \\
\pr{iii} & \tps{\brm{A} + \brm{B}} = \tp{\brm{A}} + \tp{\brm{B}} \\
\pr{iv} & \tps{\alpha \brm{A}} = \alpha \tp{\brm{A}}
\end{array}
\]

Definition 5 Symmetric tensor
A tensor \(\brm{T}\) is symmetric if \(\brm{T} = \brm{T}^{\msf{T}}\).


Definition 6 Skew-symmetric tensor
A tensor \(\brm{T}\) is skew symmetric if \(\brm{T} = -\brm{T}^{\msf{T}}\).

Every tensor can be expressed as the sum of a symmetric and skew symmetric tensor. Specifically, the symmetric part of a tensor is given by \[
    \text{sym}\pr{\brm{T}} = \frac{1}{2}\pr{\brm{T} + \brm{T}^{\msf T}}
\] and the skew-symmetric part is given by \[

title: 1 Tensors
text:
For the time being, we forgo a more precise and thorough discussion of tensors and identify them as linear maps between Euclidean vector spaces for our purposes.

Definition 1 Tensors
We refer to linear maps \(\brm{T} \in \mc{L}\pr{\b{E}^{n}, \b{F}^n}\) as tensors, where \(\b{E}^{n}\) and \(\b{F}^{n}\) are Euclidean vector spaces.

Consequentially, the previous discussion on linear maps is applicable to tensors. Important tensors that we will study in continuum mechanics include the deformation gradient tensor, velocity gradient tensor, strain tensors, stress tensors, stiffness tensors, and many more. Since tensors are linear maps, the set of all tensors between two vector spaces is also a vector space.
Some Important Tensors

Definition 2 Identity tensor
Let \(\brm{I} : \b{E}^n \ra \b{E}^n\) be such that \[
    \brm{I} \bs{v} = \bs{v}
\] for all \(\bs v \in \b{E}^n\). Then \(\brm{I}\) is called the identity tensor.

The identity tensor (previously defined as the identity map) maps every vector to itself.

Definition 3 Null tensor
Let \(\bs 0 : \b{E}^n \ra \b{F}^n\) be such that \[
    \bs{0} \bs{v} = \bs{0}_{\b F}
\] for all \(\bs v \in \b{E}^n\). Then \(\bs 0\) is called the null tensor.


Definition 4 Transpose of a tensor
The transpose of a tensor \(\brm{T}\) is the tensor \(\brm{T}^{\msf{T}}\) that obeys the following rule \[
\bs{u}\cdot\pr{\brm{T} \bs{v}} = \pr{\brm{T}^{\msf T} \bs{u}} \cdot \bs{v}
\] for all \(\bs u, \bs v \in \b E^{n}\)

Properties of Transposes
\[  
\begin{array}{ll}
\pr{i} & \tp{\pr{\tp{\brm{A}}}} = \brm{A} \\
\pr{ii} & \tp{\pr{\brm{A} \brm{B}}} = \tp{\brm{B}} \tp{\brm{A}} \\
\pr{iii} & \tps{\brm{A} + \brm{B}} = \tp{\brm{A}} + \tp{\brm{B}} \\
\pr{iv} & \tps{\alpha \brm{A}} = \alpha \tp{\brm{A}}
\end{array}
\]

Definition 5 Symmetric tensor
A tensor \(\brm{T}\) is symmetric if \(\brm{T} = \brm{T}^{\msf{T}}\).


Definition 6 Skew-symmetric tensor
A tensor \(\brm{T}\) is skew symmetric if \(\brm{T} = -\brm{T}^{\msf{T}}\).

Every tensor can be expressed as the sum of a symmetric and skew symmetric tensor. Specifically, the symmetric part of a tensor is given by \[
    \text{sym}\pr{\brm{T}} = \frac{1}{2}\pr{\brm{T} + \brm{T}^{\msf T}}
\] and the skew-symmetric part is given by \[
    \text{skew}\pr{\brm{T}} = \frac{1}{2}\pr{\brm{T} - \brm{T}^{\msf T}}
\]

title: 1 Tensors done properly
text:
We would like form a product between two vectors \(\bs{v} \in \mc{V}\) and \(\bs{w} \in \mc{W}\). We denote this product by the symbol \(\bs{v} \otimes \bs{w}\) pronounced ‘\(\bs{v}\) tensor \(\bs{w}\)’. We attach to this tensor product some distributive properties:
\[
    \begin{align*}
    \text{For } \bs{v}_{1}, \bs{v}_{2} \in \mc{V}&, \bs{w}_{1}, \bs{w}_{2} \in \mc{W}, a \in \b{R}, \\
    \pr{\bs{v}_{1} + \bs{v}_{2}} \otimes \bs{w}_1 &= \bs{v}_{1} \otimes \bs{w} + \bs{v}_{2} \otimes \bs{w}_2 \\
    \bs{v}_{1} \otimes \pr{\bs{w}_1 + \bs{w}_2} &= \bs{v}_{1} \otimes \bs{w}_2 + \bs{v}_{1} \otimes \bs{w}_2 \\
    a \pr{\bs{v}_{1} \otimes \bs{w}_{1}} &= \pr{a \bs{v}_{1}} \otimes \bs{w}_{1} = \bs{v}_{1} \otimes \pr{a \bs{w}_{1}}
    \end{align*}
\]
The formal definition of a tensor product is the following.

Definition 1 Tensor product
A tensor product \(\bs{v} \otimes \bs{w}\) is an element of the tensor product space \(\mc{V} \otimes \mc{W}\) where \(\bs{v} \in \mc{V}, \bs{w} \in \mc{W}\) and \(\mc{V} \otimes \mc{W}\) is the space of bilinear functionals \(\mc{B}\pr{\mc{V}', \mc{W}'}\). Specifically, \[
    \pr{\bs{v} \otimes \bs{w}}\pr{\bs{\varphi},\bs{\tau}} = \bs{\varphi}(\bs{v}) \bs{\tau}(\bs{w})
\] for all \(\bs{\varphi} \in \mc{V}', \bs{\tau} \in \mc{W}'\)

There exists an isomorphism between a finite dimensional inner product space and its dual space. This result is formalized through the Riesz representation theorem, which states that every continuous linear functional acting on a finite dimensional inner product space can be given by an inner product with a unique vector in that space. Then through the Riesz representation theorem, there exists a flat map the maps vectors to its covectors or dual vectors. That is, \[
    \flat : \mc{V} \ra \mc{V}'
\]
Hence, consider the following for an Euclidean vector space \(\b{E}\) and two vectors \(\bs{u}, \bs{v}, \bs{w} \in \b{E}\):
\[
    \begin{align*}
    \pr{\bs{u} \otimes \bs{v}}\pr{\cdot,\bs{w}^{\flat}} &= \bs{w}^{\flat}\pr{\bs{v}} \bs{u} = \apr{\bs{w}, \bs{v}} \bs{u} \\
    \apr{\bs{w}, \bs{v}} \bs{u} \in \mc{L}\pr{\b{E}',\b{R}}, &\text{ implying } \apr{\bs{w}, \bs{v}} \bs{u} \in \pr{\b{E}'}' = \b{E}
    \end{align*}
\]
Ultimately, we want to point out that the definition of a tensor product does not require the vector spaces to be inner product spaces. However, if they are equipped with an inner product, then there is a nice isomorphism to the dual space, known as the musical isomorphism, consisting of the flat and sharp maps that are inverses of each other.

Definition 2 A Dyadic product is a specific type of tensor product. Specifically, it is an element on the space \(\mc{V} \otimes \mc{V}'\).

A dyadic product can also be thought of as a linear map from \(\mc{V}\) to \(\mc{V}\). Let \(\mc{V}\) be an inner product space. Further, let \(\bs{u}, \bs{v} \in \mc{V}\) and \(\bs{w}^{\flat} \in \mc{V}'\). Then, \[
    \pr{\bs{v} \otimes \bs{w}^\flat} \pr{\cdot, \bs u} = \pr{\bs{w}^\flat (\bs u)} \bs{v} = \inpd{\bs{w}}{\bs u} \bs v
\]

title: 1 Maps
text:
Definition 1 Map
A map (or function) \(f : X \ra Y\) assigns each element of the set \(X\) to exactly one element of the set \(Y\). In other words, it returns a single, unique output when operated on an input.

Typically, a map \(f : \mc{D} \subset \b{R} \ra \b{R}\) that returns a real number on being fed a real number is referred to as a function. Sometimes, it can be defined by a formula, for example, as
\[
    y=f(x)
\]
where \(x \in \mc{D} \subset \b{R}\) and \(y \in \b{R}\). A distinction is made between the function \(f\) and the function’s value \(f(x)\). Some examples of functions include
\[
\begin{align*}
    y &= \sin(x), ~x \in \b{R} \\
    y &= 1/x, ~x \in \b{R} - \{0\}
\end{align*}
\]
We will refer more general operations as maps whose input and output are more general mathematical objects. Examples, of general mathematical objects can be complex numbers, plane geometric objects (triangle, circles, etc.), 3D geometric objects (cubes, spheres, ect.), digital images, and of course the main focus of this course, vectors. The only requirements on a map is that it should be well defined. That is, we should clearly know the domain of the mapping, and for each element of the domain the mapping should always return a well defined, unique object.
Examples

\(A : \mc{D} \ra \b{R}^{+}\), where \(\mc{D}\) is the set of all triangles and for each \(x \in \mc D\), \(A(x)\) returns the area of the triangle.
\(V : \mc{D} \ra \b{R}^{+}\), where \(\mc{D}\) is the set of all cubes and for each \(x \in \mc D\), \(V(x)\) returns the volume of the cube.
\(D : \mc{D} \ra \cpr{\text{Mon,Tu,Wed,Th,Fri,Sat,Sun}}\), where \(\mc{D}\) is the set of all dates and for each \(x \in \mc D\), \(D(x)\) returns the corresponding day of the week for a particular date.
\(\text{Col}: \mc{D} \ra \cpr{\text{Red,Blue,Green}}\), where \(\mc{D}\) is the set of all pixels on a well defined digital image and for each \(x \in \mc D\), \(\text{Col}(x)\) returns the pixel’s color.
Norms
Inner products

Non examples

\(V : \mc{D} \ra \b{R}^{+}\), where \(\mc D\) is the set of all words in the English language and for each \(x \in \mc D, \, V(x)\) returns to us the volume of the word. (Concept of volume is ill defined for words).
\(\text{Age} : \mc D \ra \b{R}^{+}\), where \(\mc D\) is the set of all people on Earth and for each \(x \in \mc D, \, \text{Age}(x)\) returns to use the age of a person’s child. (A person may have more than one child or no child at all).


Definition 2 Map between Euclidean spaces
The map \(\bs{T} : \b E^{n} \ra \b F^{n}\) assigns a vector \(\bs v \in \b E^n\) the unique vector \(\bs{T}(\bs{v}) \in \b{F}^n\). It is called a map between Euclidean spaces.





Definition 3 Linear map
A linear map \(\bs{T} : \mc V \ra  \mc W\) is a map from \(\mc V \ra \mc W\) with the following properties:

\(\bs{T}(\bs u + \bs v) = \bs{T}\bs{u} + \bs{T}\bs{v}\) for all \(\bs{u}, \bs{v} \in \mc{V}\)
\(\bs{T}(a \bs u) = a (\bs{T}\bs{u})\) for all \(a \in \b{R}\) and \(\bs{u} \in \mc{V}\)


\(\mc V\) and \(\mc{W}\) are called the domain and codomain of \(\bs{T}\) respectively. Linear maps are also referred to as linear transformations. Note, the definition of the addition and scalar multiplication operations may be different int the two vector spaces \(\mc{V}\) and \(\mc{W}\). We usually denote vectors by lowercase bold symbols and linear maps by uppercase bold symbols.
The set of all linear maps from \(\mc{V}\) to \(\mc{W}\) is denoted by \(\mc{L}\pr{\mc{V}, \mc{W}}\).
Examples

Identity: \(\bs{I} \bs{v} = \bs{v}\)
Multiplication by a scalar: \(\bs{T} \bs{v} = a \bs{v}\)
Differentiation: \(D f = f'\)



Definition 4 Addition and scalar multiplication on \(\mc{L}\pr{\mc{V}, \mc{W}}\)
Let \(\bs{S}, \bs{T} \in \mc{L}\pr{\mc{V}, \mc{W}}\) and \(a \in \b{R}\). Then \[
    \pr{\bs{S} + \bs{T}}\bs v = \bs{S} \bs v + \bs{T} \bs v ~~\text{and}~~ (a \bs{T})\bs v = a (\bs{T} \bs v)
\] for all \(\bs v \in \mc{V}\)

You should now be able to prove that the space of linear maps \(\mc{L}\pr{\mc{V}, \mc{W}}\) is a vector space! Therefore linear maps are also vectors! This is the reason we try to steer clear of the notion that vectors are quantities with direction and magnitude, since in reality, a vector a much more general mathematical object.
Properties of linear maps
If \(\bs{S} \in \mc{L}\pr{\mc{U}, \mc{V}}\) and \(\bs{T} \in \mc{L}\pr{\mc{V}, \mc{W}}\), then the product \(\bs{T}\bs{S} \in \mc{L}\pr{\mc{U}, \mc{W}}\), defined by \[
    \pr{\bs{T}\bs{S}}\bs{u} = \bs{T}\pr{\bs{S}\bs{u}}
\] for all \(\bs{u} \in \mc{U}\).
Linear maps obey the associative, distributive and identity properties.
Linear maps of the type \(\bs{T} : \mc{V} \ra \mc{V}\) are called linear operators, that is domain and codomain are the exact same vector space. Linear maps of the type \(\bs{T} : \mc{V} \ra \b{R}\) are called linear forms or linear functionals.

This is the reason we try to steer clear of the notion that vectors are quantities with direction and magnitude, since in reality, a vector a much more general mathematical object.
Properties of linear maps
If \(\bs{S} \in \mc{L}\pr{\mc{U}, \mc{V}}\) and \(\bs{T} \in \mc{L}\pr{\mc{V}, \mc{W}}\), then the product \(\bs{T}\bs{S} \in \mc{L}\pr{\mc{U}, \mc{W}}\), defined by \[
    \pr{\bs{T}\bs{S}}\bs{u} = \bs{T}\pr{\bs{S}\bs{u}}
\] for all \(\bs{u} \in \mc{U}\).
Linear maps obey the associative, distributive and identity properties.
Linear maps of the type \(\bs{T} : \mc{V} \ra \mc{V}\) are called linear operators, that is domain and codomain are the exact same vector space. Linear maps of the type \(\bs{T} : \mc{V} \ra \b{R}\) are called linear forms or linear functionals.

title: A continuous bijection that is not a homeomorphism
text:
2 The example

Example 1 (Wrapping an interval onto the circle) Let \(S^1 = \{ (y_1, y_2) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : y_1^2 + y_2^2 = 1 \}\) and define \[
f : [0, 2\pi) \to S^1, \qquad f(t) = (\cos t, \sin t).
\tag{1}\] Then \(f\) is a continuous bijection, but \(f^{-1}\) is not continuous at \((1, 0)\). Hence \(f\) is not a homeomorphism.







Figure 1: The map \(f\) of Eq. 1. Points \(t_n = 2\pi - 1/n\) near the excluded endpoint \(2\pi\) (red) are mapped next to \(f(0) = (1,0)\), while their preimages stay far from \(0\).




2.1 \(f\) is continuous
Its components \(\cos\) and \(\sin\) are continuous on \(\mathbb{R}\), hence on \([0, 2\pi)\).


2.2 \(f\) is injective
Suppose \(f(t_1) = f(t_2)\) with \(t_1, t_2 \in [0, 2\pi)\). Equality of cosines and sines implies \(t_1 - t_2 = 2\pi k\) for some integer \(k\). Since \(|t_1 - t_2| < 2\pi\), \(k = 0\), so \(t_1 = t_2\).


2.3 \(f\) is surjective
Every \((y_1, y_2) \in S^1\) can be written as \((\cos\theta, \sin\theta)\) for some \(\theta \in \mathbb{R}\). Subtracting a suitable integer multiple of \(2\pi\) gives such a \(\theta\) in \([0, 2\pi)\).


2.4 \(f^{-1}\) is not continuous at \((1,0)\)
Let \(g = f^{-1} : S^1 \to [0, 2\pi)\) and, for \(n \geq 1\), \[
t_n = 2\pi - \frac{1}{n} \in [0, 2\pi), \qquad p_n = f(t_n) = \left( \cos\tfrac{1}{n}, \, -\sin\tfrac{1}{n} \right).
\] Then \[
\left| p_n - (1,0) \right| = 2 \sin\frac{1}{2n} \to 0,
\] so \(p_n \to (1,0)\) in \(S^1\). However, \[
g(p_n) = 2\pi - \frac{1}{n} \to 2\pi \neq 0 = g(1,0).
\] Since \(S^1\) and \([0, 2\pi)\) are metric spaces, sequential continuity is equivalent to continuity. Therefore \(g\) is not continuous at \((1,0)\).
Figure 1 shows the mechanism: \(f\) glues the two ends of the interval together, and \(f^{-1}\) must tear them apart again.


2.5 No homeomorphism exists between these spaces
The failure is not specific to \(f\): no map \(h : S^1 \to [0, 2\pi)\) whatsoever is a homeomorphism. Two independent arguments follow.

Compactness. \(S^1\) is closed and bounded in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), hence compact. \([0, 2\pi)\) is not closed in \(\mathbb{R}\), hence not compact. A continuous image of a compact space is compact, so there is no continuous surjection \(S^1 \to [0, 2\pi)\).
Connectedness. Removing the point \(\pi\) disconnects \([0, 2\pi)\) into \([0, \pi)\) and \((\pi, 2\pi)\). Removing any point \(q\) from \(S^1\) leaves a connected set, namely the continuous image of an open interval of length \(2\pi\). A homeomorphism \(h\) would restrict to a homeomorphism between \(S^1 \setminus \{h^{-1}(\pi)\}\) and \([0, 2\pi) \setminus \{\pi\}\), which is impossible.

section: 3 When a continuous bijection is automatically a homeomorphism
text:
3 When a continuous bijection is automatically a homeomorphism
The example relies on the domain being non-compact and the map changing dimension. Removing either feature eliminates the pathology.

Theorem 1 (Compact domain, Hausdorff codomain) Let \(X\) be compact, \(Y\) Hausdorff, and \(f : X \to Y\) a continuous bijection. Then \(f\) is a homeomorphism.


Proof. It suffices to show that \(f\) maps closed sets to closed sets, because then \((f^{-1})^{-1}(C) = f(C)\) is closed for every closed \(C \subseteq X\). A closed subset \(C\) of the compact space \(X\) is compact. Its image \(f(C)\) is compact because \(f\) is continuous. A compact subset of a Hausdorff space is closed. Hence \(f(C)\) is closed.

In Example 1, \(Y = S^1\) is Hausdorff but \(X = [0, 2\pi)\) is not compact, so Thrm. 1 does not apply.

Theorem 2 (Invariance of domain (Brouwer)) Let \(U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) be open and \(f : U \to \mathbb{R}^n\) continuous and injective. Then \(f(U)\) is open and \(f : U \to f(U)\) is a homeomorphism.

The proof requires algebraic topology and is omitted. In Example 1, the domain is one-dimensional while the codomain lies in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), so Thrm. 2 does not apply.

title: A continuous bijection that is not a homeomorphism
text:
4 Relevance to continuum mechanics
A deformation \(\boldsymbol{\chi} : \mathcal{B}_0 \to \mathbb{R}^3\) is assumed continuous and injective. It is a bijection onto its image \(\mathcal{B} = \boldsymbol{\chi}(\mathcal{B}_0)\). Whether \(\boldsymbol{\chi}^{-1} : \mathcal{B} \to \mathcal{B}_0\) is also continuous is settled by the two theorems above.

If \(\mathcal{B}_0\) is an open subset of \(\mathbb{R}^3\), Thrm. 2 applies with \(n = 3\).
If \(\mathcal{B}_0\) is the closure of a bounded open set, it is compact. Since \(\mathbb{R}^3\) is Hausdorff, Thrm. 1 applies.

In either case, \(\boldsymbol{\chi}\) is a homeomorphism onto \(\mathcal{B}\). Material points that are close in the current configuration were close in the reference configuration, and the inverse motion \(\mathbf{X} = \boldsymbol{\chi}^{-1}(\mathbf{x})\) is continuous. Example 1 shows that this conclusion is a genuine consequence of the setting, not a property of every continuous bijection.
